paras: The whitecap attack on the home of Eli Hilson was a night shooting in November 1903 in which a band of whitecaps fired into the house of Eli Hilson, a Black farmer living about seven miles from Brookhaven in Lincoln County, Mississippi, after he had ignored their warning to leave. No one was hit, although Hilson's wife had given birth only hours before. The papers reported it as part of a revival of whitecapping that within days killed another Black farmer, Henry Lisle, and recalled it when Hilson himself was shot dead the next month.

A New Orleans dispatch of November 21 reported that whitecaps were "again at work" around McCall Creek in Lincoln, Franklin and Amite counties, ordering residents away, and that Senator McGee of Franklin had laid several cases of violence before Gov. Longino. In Brookhaven, the Leader recalled that after "last summer's campaign" people in a position to know had said the whitecap organization in the county had disbanded.
Hilson owned his farm and was described as prosperous. According to the Leader, the whitecaps had warned him "last winter" to leave, and he had disregarded the warning.

On a Saturday night, which the Leader's issue of November 28 called "last Saturday night," whitecaps visited Hilson's home and "literally riddled his house" with bullets. A New Orleans dispatch in the New York Sun described the attackers as "a large body of armed Whitecaps on horseback" calling on Black residents who had been ordered to leave the county and had stayed. The Leader later wrote that "several volleys" were fired into the house while Hilson's wife lay sick in bed with an infant only a few hours old. None of the family was hit, an escape the Leader called "almost a miracle."

A few days later the whitecappers returned to the house of Henry Lisle (also printed Liste and List), a Black farmer in the Gum Grove neighborhood whose house had been shot into two weeks before, and killed him.

No report of arrests for the attack on Hilson's house appears in the coverage. The New Orleans dispatch said public sentiment in the county was "strongly against the Whitecappers" and that Gov. Longino had promised to take action.

Hilson remained on his place. On a Saturday evening in December, driving home alone in his buggy from Brookhaven, he was shot dead about a quarter of a mile from his house. Coroner Geo. Lambright, Jr., held an inquest whose jury found that he died of a gunshot wound "at the hands of parties unknown," and the Leader counted him as the second Black man murdered by whitecaps in that part of the county within a month.

In the days after the attack only white papers reported it. The Leader ran the first account under the headline "MORE WHITE CAPPING IN LINCOLN," spoke of Hilson as "the negro," and warned that whitecapping was "assuming a graver and more aggravated form." The New York Sun carried a New Orleans dispatch headlined "WHITECAPS' TERRORISM" with the subhead "Negroes Persecuted," in which Hilson's house was a brief mention in a story centered on Lisle's death. Within a week the Leader's story was reprinted, credited only to "a dispatch from Brookhaven," in the Brandon News, the Port Gibson Reveille and the Greene County Herald under the headline "'NIGHT RIDERS' RIOT AGAIN."

The attack reached the Black press only after Hilson's murder, when the Baltimore Afro-American printed a New Orleans dispatch under the headline "MURDERED BY WHITE CAPS" that retold the night shooting. Its text closely follows the Leader's December article but calls Hilson "colored" rather than "a negro" and adds that "The colored people are greatly alarmed and are deserting the county." The Leader's December article condemned the "dastardly white cap outrages" for their cost in farm labor and credit as well as on "considerations of humanity."

The date of the attack is given only relatively. The Leader's contemporaneous "last Saturday night," in an issue dated November 28, points to November 21; the December accounts' "three or four weeks ago" and "Three weeks ago" are looser. The first report put the farm seven miles from Brookhaven, the December accounts eight.

accounts.label: Local paper (Brookhaven Leader)
accounts.gist: On 'last Saturday night' whitecaps visited Hilson, who had been warned to vacate, and 'literally riddled his house with bulets'; none of the family was hit though his wife had a baby a few hours old.

accounts.label: New Orleans wire
accounts.gist: Negroes ordered to leave and failing to do so were visited at night by a large body of armed whitecaps on horseback; Hilson's house was riddled, no one killed, and Lisle's house was visited next and Lisle killed.

accounts.label: Retrospective after Hilson's murder
accounts.gist: Hilson, warned the winter before, had his house fired into with 'several volleys' about three weeks earlier while his wife lay sick with a newborn; he stayed and was then assassinated.

framing.detail: The Leader headlined 'MORE WHITE CAPPING IN LINCOLN.', called the family's escape 'almost a miracle', and said whitecapping was 'assuming a graver and more aggravated form'.
The New York Sun ran the New Orleans dispatch as 'WHITECAPS' TERRORISM' with the subhead 'Negroes Persecuted' and reported public sentiment against the whitecaps.
Three Mississippi weeklies reprinted the Leader's account as '"NIGHT RIDERS" RIOT AGAIN' within a week.

After Hilson's murder the Leader called the 'dastardly white cap outrages' a 'disgraceful state of affairs', stressing lost farm labor, foreclosures and credit as well as 'considerations of humanity'.
The Afro-American recounted the night attack only within its report of the murder, headlined 'MURDERED BY WHITE CAPS', and added that Black residents were 'deserting the county'.

versions.value: 'last Saturday night' in the Leader issue dated Nov. 28 (Nov. 21)
'About three or four weeks ago' (Leader, Dec. 23) / 'Three weeks ago' (New Orleans dispatch of Dec. 22)

conflicts.note: The contemporaneous local report is the better evidence; the December recollections are approximate. The Leader's own dating of the Lisle killing ('following Thursday night (Nov. 24)') is inconsistent, since Nov. 24, 1903 was a Tuesday, and the reprints say 'Tuesday night' (A4).
Minor; both place the farm in southwestern Lincoln County near Brookhaven.
The reprints' 'horse' is a misprint of the Leader's 'house'; all other accounts say the house.
